content: This updated review examines the potential link between ovarian stimulating drugs used for infertility treatment and the risk of ovarian cancer, including both invasive ovarian cancer and borderline ovarian tumors. The review builds upon the original Cochrane Review from 2013, incorporating additional studies published between February 2013 and November 2018. The evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach to determine the certainty of findings. The review included 13 case-control studies and 24 cohort studies, involving a total of 4,684,724 women. Two cohort studies reported an increased incidence of invasive ovarian cancer in subfertile women exposed to fertility drugs compared to unexposed women. One study found a standardized incidence ratio (SIR) of 1.19 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.54 to 2.25) based on 17 cancer cases. Another study reported a hazard ratio (HR) of 1.93 (95% CI 1.18 to 3.18), with a higher risk observed in women who remained nulligravid after using clomiphene citrate (HR 2.49, 95% CI 1.30 to 4.78) compared to multiparous women (HR 1.52, 95% CI 0.67 to 3.42). However, the certainty of this evidence was rated as very low. A slight increase in ovarian cancer risk was noted among women undergoing one to three cycles of in vitro fertilization (IVF), but this finding was not statistically significant (P = 0.18). Additionally, no increased risk of invasive ovarian cancer was observed in women with BRCA mutations who used infertility drugs, based on one cohort and one case-control study. For borderline ovarian tumors, one cohort study reported an increased risk in women exposed to fertility drugs, with an SIR of 3.61 (95% CI 1.45 to 7.44). This risk was particularly elevated after treatment with clomiphene citrate (SIR 7.47, 95% CI 1.54 to 21.83) based on 12 cases. Another cohort study found an increased risk of borderline ovarian tumors in subfertile women treated with IVF compared to those not treated with IVF, with an HR of 4.23 (95% CI 1.25 to 14.33) after more than one year of follow-up. A large cohort study also reported an increased risk of borderline ovarian tumors, with an HR of 2.46 (95% CI 1.20 to 5.04), based on 17 cases. One study identified a significant increase in serous borderline ovarian tumors after the use of progesterone for more than four cycles, with a risk ratio (RR) of 2.63 (95% CI 1.04 to 6.64). A case-control study reported an increased risk of borderline ovarian tumors after clomiphene citrate use, with an SIR of 2.5 (95% CI 1.3 to 4.5) based on 11 cases. Another study found an elevated risk associated with human menopausal gonadotropin use, with an odds ratio (OR) of 9.38 (95% CI 1.66 to 52.08). However, one study estimated an increased risk of borderline ovarian tumors based on only four cases, with no control group reporting fertility drug use. The certainty of evidence for these findings was consistently rated as very low. While some studies suggested a slight increase in the risks of ovarian cancer and borderline ovarian tumors, none provided moderateor high-certainty evidence. The authors concluded that the available evidence remains insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the relationship between infertility drugs and ovarian cancer risk. The findings suggest a slightly higher risk in nulliparous women compared to multiparous women and for borderline ovarian tumors, but the small number of cancer cases and limited information on drug type or dosage preclude strong conclusions.
